title: Annotations as Rollouts: Cheaper RL for Video Models
hook: RL post-training wastes most of its samples on bad rollouts. OraRL drops the ground-truth annotation into the group as an oracle rollout — and has to fix the advantage math to make it work.
key_points: Standard on-policy RL for video MLLMs samples groups where few rollouts are good enough to learn from.
OraRL injects each dataset annotation into the on-policy group as an 'oracle rollout' — a direct positive target.
Naively adding a high-reward oracle raises the group baseline and flips real positives negative; the authors call this advantage inversion.
Their fix: an oracle-free baseline from policy rollouts, plus a separate detached oracle advantage and a directional gain term.
Sign-balanced pruning keeps only the oracle and the strongest rollout of each sign — 2.2x SFT step time vs 4.9x for GRPO with chain-of-thought.
Video-ORA-9B decodes in 130 ms instead of 4,780 ms without CoT, and scores 73.1 on VSI-Bench vs 55.0 for GPT-5.
content_html: Video multimodal LLMs are usually post-trained with on-policy RL, but sampling a group of rollouts is wasteful — most come back too weak to teach anything, and generating chain-of-thought for each one is expensive. Li and colleagues point out that the dataset already contains a perfect rollout: the annotation itself. OraRL feeds that annotation into the on-policy group as an oracle rollout, a direct positive target rather than just a scoring reference.
extra_html:
The catch, and the fix

You cannot simply drop a high-reward sequence into a group. Because group-relative methods compute each rollout's advantage against the group mean, an oracle with near-perfect reward pulls the baseline up and turns genuinely good policy rollouts into negatives — what the authors name advantage inversion. OraRL decouples the estimator: policy rollouts alone set the baseline, while the oracle–policy gap contributes a directional gain and a separate, detached oracle advantage.

What it buys

Sign-balanced pruning keeps only the oracle and the strongest rollouts of each sign, cutting step time to about 2.2x SFT versus 4.9x for GRPO with chain-of-thought. The authors report gains that hold from 0.8B to 9B and up to 100k prompts, and their Video-ORA-9B skips CoT entirely — decoding in 130 ms instead of 4,780 ms while improving temporal, tracking, and segmentation scores over the prior best models.

related.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
related.hook: DeepSeek shows strong reasoning can emerge from RL on verifiable rewards with minimal supervised data - and those reasoning traces can be distilled into smaller models.

flashcards.back_html: Dropping a high-reward oracle rollout into an on-policy group raises the group's baseline, which turns otherwise-positive policy advantages negative — the model gets punished for good rollouts.

flashcards.prompt: How does OraRL use dataset annotations differently from standard RL post-training?

choices.text: It puts the annotation into the on-policy group as an extra rollout to optimize toward
It uses annotations only to score the sampled rollouts
It replaces the reward model with an annotation classifier
It filters out any prompt whose annotation is ambiguous

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper's core observation is that annotations can serve as oracle rollouts — direct positive optimization targets — not just as scoring signal.

flashcards.prompt: Why is OraRL cheaper per step than GRPO with chain-of-thought?
flashcards.back_html: Sign-balanced pruning keeps only the oracle and the strongest rollouts of each sign, and the model skips costly CoT generation: 2.2x SFT step time versus GRPO-with-CoT's 4.9x.
